papers.title: Genome-wide chromatin accessibility during early embryogenesis in a generalist cichlid fish
papers.abstract: Background Lake Malawi's haplochromine cichlids are one of the most rapid and species-rich vertebrate adaptive radiations known, generating hundreds of species within < 1 million years, yet how regulatory regions shape their embryonic development remains poorly understood. Astatotilapia calliptera, a generalist riverine lineage and proxy for the ancestral stock that seeded this radiation, offers a developmental chromatin baseline against which regulatory divergence in specialised lineages can be compared. Results We generated genome-wide ATAC-seq profiles of A. calliptera embryos across three developmental stages (3, 7 and 12 days post-fertilisation, dpf), identifying 550,876-701,889 accessible chromatin peaks per stage. Accessible chromatin was enriched at gene promoters and at both highly conserved and accelerated conserved noncoding elements at every stage. The functional repertoire of accessible-promoter genes shifted across development, from early patterning at 3 dpf to the broadest regulatory repertoire at 7 dpf, and an increasingly neural- and locomotory-behaviour-enriched repertoire by 12 dpf, coinciding with post-hatching motor maturation. Differential accessibility showed that chromatin opening, rather than closing, dominates the earliest transitions (3 vs 7 and 3 vs 12 dpf), driven mostly by general metabolic genes, whereas the smaller, later 7 vs 12 dpf transition combined targeted gains at tissue-remodelling and apoptosis genes with losses at genes governing early neural and retinal patterning; almost all of these losses (96%) were at promoters that had opened between 3 and 7 dpf, indicating transient rather than sustained opening. Transcription factor (TF) footprinting identified stage-specific regulatory activity among developmentally important TFs, while the broader TF-promoter network remained topologically stable across all three stages, built around conserved hub regulators of core neural and sensory patterning genes e.g., SOX2, FOXG1, PTF1A, SOX10. This suggests that wiring is established early and largely maintained, following the hourglass model, with developmental progression driven by changes in activity of this conserved programme. Conclusions Together, these findings establish the first embryonic epigenomic resource for A. calliptera, revealing a developmental chromatin landscape of broad early opening and progressive functional specialisation, and providing a comparative framework for understanding how regulatory evolution has shaped Lake Malawi cichlid diversification.

papers.title: Salinity adaptation in date palm (Phoenix dactylifera): evidence for selective sweeps at Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) genes
papers.abstract: The date palm is a high salinity tolerant fruit tree grown mainly in the region spanning from North Africa to parts of South Asia. Climate change models of this region indicate the possibility of increasing salinity in the future. The Salt Overly Sensitive (SOS) pathway is crucial for salinity tolerance in plants, serving as a primary defense mechanism by facilitating sodium exclusion. To better understand date palms' salt tolerance, we analyzed variation in SOS pathway genes in a set of 197 date palm genomes collected from across the range of cultivation. Here, we show evidence for selective sweeps in multiple SOS pathway genes. A single major pdSOS1 haplotype is at very high frequency in Eastern and Western subpopulations, with a minor, likely ancestral haplotype still present in both geographical locations. Allele-specific gene expression analysis showed differences in salt-treated roots between swept and ancestral haplotypes. Interestingly, sequence-based analysis of the pdSOS1 haplotype suggested a second, much earlier introgression event between P. theophrasti and date palm, though direction is unclear. This event happened before both the selective sweep and the previously reported recent introgression to date palm. We identified a MITE transposable element inserted into a pdSOS1 intron on the swept haplotype, and a similar insertion was found in an intron of the SOS2 paralog pdCIPK8. Both insertions are unique to date palm among Phoenix species. The pdCIPK8 haplotype containing the MITE is also at high frequency in both populations. Further analysis showed evidence for a selective sweep spanning the pdSOS3 region in the western population that shares similarity to an Eastern haplotype spanning the promoter region only. Slower extended haplotype homozygosity decay surrounding the genes in the western population suggests that the swept haplotype originated in the East and spread to the West in all cases. Altogether, our data provide evidence of selective sweeps in the date palm SOS pathway and may go to explaining how this species has developed such high salinity tolerance.

papers.title: Genome evolution and glycosyltransferase diversification shape asperosaponin biosynthesis in Dipsacus asperoides
papers.abstract: Deciphering the genomic and enzymatic features associated with high-abundance specialized metabolism is important for understanding and engineering bioactive natural product biosynthesis. Asperosaponin , a hederagenin-based saponin, accumulates at exceptionally high levels in Dipsacus asperoides roots and is by far the predominant triterpenoid saponin. Here, by integrating a chromosome-level genome assembly with comparative genomics, transcriptomics, metabolite profiling, and biochemical characterization, we reconstructed a major biosynthetic route to asperosaponin and identified diversification of triterpenoid-associated gene families. Functional analyses revealed an ordered glycosylation sequence in which DaUGT73GZ2 preferentially accepts C-3-glycosylated substrates retaining a free C-28 carboxyl group, thereby establishing a C-3-before-C-28 glycosylation order during asperosaponin biosynthesis. Phylogenetic and biochemical analyses further uncovered functional differentiation among UGT85CA enzymes involved in C-3 arabinosylation, while genomic and expression analyses revealed lineage-specific patterns of pathway gene duplication and transcriptional regulation. Together, these findings identify genomic, enzymatic, and transcriptional features associated with the distinctive, high-abundance triterpenoid saponin profile of D. asperoides roots and provide a framework for understanding and engineering triterpenoid saponin biosynthesis.

papers.title: WheatPanRef: a unified linear pan-reference genome for wheat genomics
papers.abstract: Linear reference genomes provide coordinates for read mapping, variant discovery and multi-omics data integration, yet assembly-specific coordinate systems limit data reuse, particularly in the large, repetitive and polyploid wheat genome. Here, we present WheatPanRef, a scalable linear pan-reference and coordinate framework that integrates wheat sequence diversity within a stable coordinate system. We reconciled independent Chinese Spring assemblies by resolving structural and sequences discrepancies to constructed a 14.50-Gb consensus sequences CS-NP. Using CS-NP as backbone, we incorporated 4.37 Gb of non-redundant non-CS sequences from 37 diverse wheat accessions, generating WheatPanRef (18.87 Gb). WheatPanRef improves read-alignment performance and captures putative wild-relative introgressions and sequences absent or unanchored in conventional references. Bidirectional coordinate-translation system enables accurate projection between WheatPanRef and individual assemblies without remapping, facilitating genomic resource integration and reuse. WheatPanRef provides a common sequence and coordinate foundation for population-scale wheat genomics, with potential utility for genomic resource integration in other complex crops.

papers.title: Mapping the regulatory wiring of endothelial cell differentiation reveals a critical role for Hippo mechanosignaling
papers.abstract: At each step of development, stem cells encounter a branching decision to differentiate into one type of cell or another. This decision is executed through the action of competing gene programs that specify different cellular identities. Consequently, creating a comprehensive map of the gene programs that drive each branching step of human cell differentiation remains a long-sought goal of developmental and stem cell biology. Here, we introduce a framework combining genome-wide CRISPR screens, single-cell readouts, and gene program inference to systematically discover and characterize regulators of cell differentiation. This framework includes a method for CRISPR perturbations paired with single-cell RNA-seq called circular capture Perturb-seq (CC-Perturb-seq), which improves gRNA detection from split-pool combinatorial indexing protocols and enables perturbing many candidate regulators to map their effects on gene programs. We applied this framework to map how human pluripotent stem cells differentiate into arterial endothelial cells (ECs), and identified 174 regulators that promote or inhibit EC differentiation. By tracking gene programs across three stages of differentiation, we resolved when and how regulators divert cells toward alternative fates. This map revealed an unexpected requirement for the Hippo mechanosignaling pathway in EC specification. During lateral mesoderm differentiation, Hippo mechanosignaling was required to activate ETV2, the master transcriptional regulator of endothelial identity. Inhibiting Hippo blocked ETV2 even in the presence of VEGF and diverted progenitors to a mesenchymal fate in vitro. Likewise, Hippo signaling was required for maximal etv2 expression in developing zebrafish embryos. Conversely, pharmacologically activating the Hippo pathway increased the purity of both arterial and venous EC differentiation in vitro. Our framework thus identifies novel regulators of endothelial cell differentiation, improves stem-cell differentiation protocols via manipulation of mechanosignaling, and provides a generalizable platform for mapping the regulatory wiring of human development.

papers.title: NanoPAMDA enables rapid PAM characterization of metagenome-derived Cas9 effectors
papers.abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 orthologs remain functionally underexplored despite the rapidly growing scale of publicly available metagenomic sequencing data. Here, we applied a multi-stage computational discovery pipeline to two independent sources of metagenomic sequence data, a multi-biome collection of 660,185 metagenome-assembled genomes spanning 17 public catalogs, and raw sequencing reads from human microbiome studies assembled de novo, to identify novel Cas9 orthologs. Candidates were filtered for guide RNA architectural plausibility, sequence novelty, conservation of catalytic residues, and structural integrity, yielding 14 candidates spanning both data sources for experimental characterization. To determine PAM preference at scale, we developed a cost-effective Nanopore long-read-based adaptation of the high-throughput PAM determination assay (NanoPAMDA), enabling rapid, time-resolved, kinetic PAM profiling across many candidates in parallel. One Cas9 effector, E10, showed PAM-specific activity in vitro and was catalytically active in E. coli. Together, these findings demonstrate a scalable, long-read sequencing-based framework for discovering and biochemically characterizing novel Cas9 orthologs from metagenomic data.

papers.title: Highly prevalent cargo genes of F plasmids harbored in pathogenic Escherichia coli
papers.abstract: Analysis of prevalent orthogroups (OGs) in a collection of F plasmids from extraintestinal Escherichia coli ST131 isolates has led to the identification of two groups of previously uncharacterized cargo genes that may be widely distributed among F plasmids of pathogenic E. coli. Group 1 comprises four OGs whose encoded proteins are predicted to be involved in transport-related functions. The corresponding genes cluster with other genes associated with metabolism and are highly prevalent in extraintestinal ST131 isolates. Group 2 comprises several OGs whose encoded proteins currently have unknown functions. These OGs are present in a large proportion of F plasmids from both intestinal and extraintestinal E. coli isolates. The corresponding genes cluster within an F-plasmid region that also contains genes involved in DNA metabolism, suggesting that the proteins encoded by these newly identified OGs may likewise contribute to F-plasmid DNA biology. Characterizing the functions of these newly identified proteins may improve our understanding of the contribution of F plasmid to E. coli virulence and reveal novel targets for antimicrobial intervention, either by limiting F-plasmid dissemination among multidrug-resistant (MDR) E. coli strains or by directly targeting plasmid-carrying bacteria.

papers.title: Epigenetic reprogramming by promoter hypomethylation is linked to aberrant gene expression and transcriptomic plasticity in colorectal cancer
papers.abstract: Colorectal cancer (CRC) has high phenotypic plasticity, but regulatory mechanisms of aberrant cell states are not well described. We investigated DNA methylation-based regulation of cancer cell-intrinsic transcriptomic heterogeneity in 1,183 multiregional primary tumor samples, liver metastases and tumor organoids. Most genes with strong methylation-transcriptomic association reflected canonical promoter hypermethylation and expression repression related to the CpG island methylator phenotype (CIMP). However, promoter hypomethylation and overexpression of APOLD1 and ELF5 identified two largely non-overlapping subgroups of canonical CIMP-negative CRCs enriched with stem-like and transit-amplifying cell states. APOLD1 tumors were further highly proliferative while ELF5 tumors were slow-cycling and associated with good survival in early-stage disease. Target genes showed patient-specific expression changes in matched primary-metastasis samples, and ELF5 aberrant metastases showed ex vivo sensitivity to putative targeting of stem cells by PI3K/mTOR inhibition, fetal de-differentiation and transition into non-canonical intestinal states. This implicates focal promoter hypomethylation in phenotypic plasticity in CRC metastasis.

papers.title: A Distinct Mode of Chromosome-End Genome Instability Revealed by Circulome Characterization and Analyses
papers.abstract: Genome instability is a central hallmark of cancer and it is characterized largely from sequence: mutation, copy-number change and rearrangement scored against a linear reference. The genome has additional degrees of freedom, such as the physical form (topology) of the DNA itself. A specific mode of localized genome dynamics changes both dimensions (sequence and topology) at once: defined chromosomal regions are also represented as extrachromosomal circular DNA (eccDNA). The biogenesis of eccDNA is a feature of many cancers, supplying the tumor with genetic elements that can participate in phenotypic selection, and supplying the observer with a window into the genomic instability landscape. Genome-wide maps of where these circles arise have not been available at scale or at high resolution. Building such maps requires physical selection of circular species, because most sequenced reads from unselected DNA derive from unrearranged sequence, conflating the signal from dynamic rearrangements with that from bulk chromosomal DNA. Here we combine biophysical and biochemical isolation of circular DNA with next-generation sequencing, applying it to a panel of cancer cell lines and to patient tumors, with non-cancerous cells and adjacent normal tissues as controls. The resulting genome-wide maps of the circular-element repertoire, the Circulome, reveal a consistent and previously unreported enrichment of these elements at particular chromosome ends. The circles map to regions extending well past the telomeres, reaching varying distances up to tens of megabases inward. This activity is accompanied by corroborating rearrangements within the linear genome, consistent with regions of chromosomal instability. Together these features define a spatially localized mode of instability in cancer, which we term Erosion at Distal Genomic Ends (EDGE). We formulate a classification problem to discriminate bladder tumor from matched normal tissue, finding that the EDGE signal outperforms the mean of all interior chromosomal regions, for each chromosome. These findings define a distinct spatial signature of cancer chromosome instability detectable through Circulome analysis, and connect early models of region-specific instability to the human cancer genome.

papers.title: A Bias Correction Method for Substructure Estimation with Small Reference Sample Sizes
papers.abstract: Reference data are important for accurate estimation of population substructure, yet sufficiently large reference samples are often unavailable for some populations. This limitation is especially important for methods that estimate population substructure from genetic summary data using reference allele frequencies derived from reference samples, such as Summix2. Here, we systematically evaluated how reference sample size for five continental reference groups [African (AFR), East Asian (EAS), European (EUR), Indigenous American (IAM), and South Asian (SAS)] affects Summix2 substructure estimates in simulated Latino-like, African American-like, and Peruvian-like populations, as well as real African American genetic data. We show that small reference sample sizes introduce systematic bias in substructure proportion estimates. We identified a sample size threshold of 150 individuals per reference group for accurate estimates with a mean estimation error below 0.05. We also developed two bias corrections: a simple inverse sample size correction and a flexible power-law correction. The power-law correction provided the greatest reduction in mean estimation error when all reference groups had small reference sample sizes, whereas the simple inverse sample size correction performed better when a single reference group had a small reference sample size. These findings provide practical guidance and bias adjustments for reliable population substructure estimation from genetic summary data, particularly when reference populations have small sample sizes.

papers.title: Unprecedented urban freshwater microviral survey highlights shift from sewage to river water communities
papers.abstract: Microviruses are abundant yet still poorly resolved components of virosphere, particularly across urban freshwater continua. Here, we investigated complete microvirus genomes recovered from sewage water (SW), treated wastewater (TW), and river water (RW) along an urban SW TW RW continuum, providing an extensive genomic dataset of 18,449 complete genomes grouped into 825 genera. This catalog enabled a high-resolution assessment of microvirus diversity, taxonomy, and ecological distribution across anthropized aquatic compartments. All currently described microvirus orders were detected, with Gokushovirales dominating the dataset and Betagokushoviridae emerging as the most prevalent family in TW and RW samples. In contrast, Alpavirales were enriched in SW but strongly depleted after treatment, consistent with their association with gut-related bacterial hosts. Alpha- and beta-diversity analyses showed that water type was the main driver of microvirus community structure, whereas seasonal effects were weak and not robust under the hydrological conditions of the sampling year. Wastewater treatment plants thus acted as strong biological filters, reshaping viral assemblages and selecting compartment-specific microvirus populations. Finally, the pronounced and reproducible shifts observed across the continuum suggest that selected microvirus groups may serve as promising bioindicators of anthropogenic influence in freshwater systems.

papers.title: De novo genome assembly of the floating-hook moss Warnstorfia fluitans
papers.abstract: The floating-hook moss Warnstorfia fluitans is a natural species dominant in subarctic and Arctic aquatic ecosystems. It is adapted to cold, acidic, and nutrient-deficient environments and possesses great potential for bioremediation by removing contaminants from polluted water in cold climate conditions. Here, we present the first de novo genome assembly of W. fluitans generated from pooled male and female gametophytes. The assembly is 725.04 Mb, has a N50 of 193.5 kb, a BUSCO completeness of 97.6% against the Viridiplantae lineage and 82% against the Embryophyta lineage. The whole assembly has Merqury quality value of 37 and Merqury completeness of 92%. A total of 30421 protein coding genes were predicted, with 78.62% completeness by compleasm and 87% OMArk completeness against the Embryophyta lineage. Repetitive sequences comprise 56.16% of the genome. We also present here the two complete circular chloroplast genomes and a linear mitochondrial genome of W. fluitans. This genomic resource will facilitate studies of ecological adaptation and a wide range of biological and evolutionary studies in bryophytes.

papers.title: A chromosome-level genome assembly of an endangered large carnivore, the wolverine, Gulo gulo gulo (Linnaeus, 1758)
papers.abstract: We describe a chromosome-level, haplotype-resolved genome assembly from a male wolverine (Gulo gulo gulo). The assembly comprises two pseudo-haplotypes of 2,523.2 Mb and 2,288.4 Mb, with 95.8% and 97.8% scaffolded into 20 autosomal chromosomes and sex chromosomes (placed in haplotype one). Assembly completeness is high (BUSCO 98.2% and 88.9%), with 20,337 and 17,692 annotated protein-coding genes for haplotypes one and two, respectively. Compared to existing wolverine genomes, the current genome is more complete and contains both sex chromosomes. This reference genome will be an important resource for population studies and conservation biology of this large carnivore.

papers.title: Leveraging short and long-read sequencing to comprehensively characterize alternatively polyadenylated and alternatively spliced transcripts
papers.abstract: Pre-mRNA processing through alternative splicing and alternative polyadenylation generates diverse transcripts from the same gene. Alternative splicing involves use of different exons and specific 3'Untranslated regions (3'UTRs). When limited to the same terminal exon, 3'end formation through alternative polyadenylation gives rise to transcripts containing 3'UTRs of different sizes which affect their subcellular localization, stability, and translatability. The full repertoire of transcripts arising from alternative pre-mRNA processing under different biological and disease states remains unknown. Using the blood cancer, mantle cell lymphoma's (MCL) as our experimental model we found that two genes, SOX11 and ATM, that contribute to the disease pathology, express transcripts that have short 3'UTRs. Apart from select transcripts, our analysis of short-read sequencing data did not uncover widespread global shortening of 3'UTRs in MCL. However, we discovered that both the canonical and non-canonical polyadenylation signals (PASs), were used for 3'end formation. We experimentally verified the PASs used by specific transcripts. Combining short-read and long-read sequencing data enabled us to characterize, classify and identify alternatively splicing in MCL. We identified splice variants for several genes including PTEN, EZH2 and validated the expression of GLS1 at the protein level and by using GLS1 inhibitors. Collectively, our approach provide insights into how to identify alternatively spliced and alternatively polyadenylated transcripts.

papers.title: GeneFamHunter: annotation-independent recovery of divergent and tandemly arrayed gene-family members from genome assemblies
papers.abstract: Motivation: Gene families expand by tandem duplication, diverge and decay, so their members are often missing, fragmented or fused in automated genome annotations, and divergent copies escape pairwise similarity searches. These challenges are particularly pronounced in non-model organisms, for which well-annotated genomes and reference proteomes are often unavailable, limiting the applicability of protein-based gene family recovery methods. Results: We developed GeneFamHunter to recover gene-family members directly from nucleotide assemblies. It searches continuous six-frame translations of overlapping genomic windows using four complementary domain- and profile-based methods, clusters hits while distinguishing tandem paralogs, predicts and validates gene models, and constructs gene trees. Across six Quest for Orthologs genomes, window-based HMMER searches recovered all 130 reference papain-like (C1A) loci, with 21 off-target hits, compared with 45 for stop-to-stop ORF searches; whole-contig HMMER searches recovered 108 (83.1%). With 11 distantly related queries, PSI-BLAST and DELTA-BLAST recovered all reference loci, whereas RPSTBLASTN recovered 98.5-99.2% and TBLASTN, as used by BITACORA, recovered 94.6-95.4%. Across six mite genomes, GeneFamHunter recovered all 209 previously reported C1 loci and identified 37 additional candidate loci. In a separate comparison, it recovered all 128 reference UniProt C1A proteins and identified five additional loci without annotated gene models; OrthoFinder included 35 non-C1A proteins, whereas OMA recovered 98 reference proteins. Availability and implementation: GeneFamHunter is implemented in Bash for Linux and SLURM clusters and is freely available at https://github.itap.purdue.edu/HeLab/GeneFamHunter (MIT license). Benchmark code and data: https://github.itap.purdue.edu/HeLab/GeneFamHunter_benchmarks and Zenodo (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.23744704).

papers.title: Four genome assemblies of new wild Gossypium hirsutum accessions from the Yucatan Peninsula, the center of domestication
papers.abstract: Gossypium hirsutum is a leading source of natural cotton fiber, accounting for most of the market share. While domestication and improvement have led to significant gains in fiber quantity and quality, the narrow germplasm base of modern cultivars creates vulnerabilities, including to emerging pests. Wild populations provide a reservoir for genetic diversity that may be valuable in identifying and transferring resistance or stress-adaptation alleles to modern breeding lines. Here we report four new genome assemblies of G. hirsutum representing distinct populations from its center of diversity in Yucatan, Mexico. These chromosome-level assemblies are highly contiguous and structurally similar to existing G. hirsutum genomes; however, comparative analyses highlight their distinctiveness, suggesting they form a valuable reservoir of untapped diversity. Preliminary analyses of nucleotide-binding leucine-rich repeat (NLR) immune receptor genes underscore this variation, suggesting presence-absence variation may exist among populations. These findings demonstrate the potential of these new genomic resources for discovery of novel disease resistance alleles and, generally, for expanding the narrow germplasm base of the modern cotton cultivars.

papers.title: High-throughput sequencing of unmethylated DNA (UMR-seq) reveals extensive epigenetic variation in the hypomethylome of diverse plant species
papers.abstract: The unmethylated regions (UMRs) in a genome can reveal the location of genes and gene regulatory loci. However, discovering UMR variation across and between entire genomes and disentangling the contribution of genetics and epigenetics to traits are challenging because they require separate and costly whole-DNA methylome and whole-genome genetic analyses. In many species this is prohibitively expensive for even a small number of samples, curtailing analysis on a population or breeding scale. Here we introduce UMR-seq, a method for the specific capture of UMRs from a genome and simultaneous sequencing of genetic variants in a single economical and scalable assay. UMR-seq charts the hypomethylome, revealing that it is highly enriched with functionally important regulatory loci. While UMRs are highly stable between vegetative tissues in plants, we find they are dynamic in the endosperm and vary substantially between accessions. Adaptable to diverse species, using this method we uncover a positive correlation between gene number in a species and UMR content, reflecting gene regulatory space in a genome. At 1/50th of the conventional cost of methylome sequencing in wheat, UMR-seq enables simultaneous population scale analysis of genetic and epigenetic variation in the functional genomic space. We reveal that in a panel of 187 elite wheat cultivars, profiling UMR variation improved genomic prediction across population groups, and UMR-based association mapping identified trait associations that were largely distinct from those detected with SNPs, providing new opportunities to understand trait biology and to enhance predictive breeding.

papers.title: Predicting single-molecule chromatin distribution from DNA sequence
papers.abstract: Genome regulation unfolds through dynamic and stochastic single-molecule events. Deep learning models that read gene regulatory activities from DNA sequences have markedly advanced our ability to predict cell-population-level averages. However, they cannot capture the full spectrum of heterogeneity and dynamics at the single-molecule level, which directly reflect the underlying mechanisms of genome regulation. Here, we introduce a sequence-to-distribution (S2d) framework that directly models the entire probabilistic distribution of single-molecule chromatin states from DNA sequence alone. We used this framework to train Mola, a model of single-molecule chromatin accessibility. We harness Mola to investigate sequence-based regulatory code and mechanisms for multiple aspects of chromatin regulation at the single-molecule level. By quantifying sequence-driven nucleosome regulation, we reveal distinct modes of transcription factor engagement with nucleosomes, including a novel nucleosome-trapping factor, ZNF146. We characterized the sequence determinants governing the +1 nucleosome after transcription start sites and identified YY1 as the strongest +1 nucleosome-positioning factor. Leveraging long-context single-molecule modeling, we further discovered a shared sequence basis for the co-accessibility of regulatory elements and the co-footprinting of transcription factors. Joint prediction of DNA methylation and accessibility reveals a sequence-driven bimodal state mediated by methylation-sensitive transcription factors. Beyond static single-molecule snapshots, the S2d framework can generate pseudo-dynamic trajectories of chromatin states and propose a roadmap toward genome-wide chromatin dynamics. Moreover, we showed that Mola can predict and interpret the effects of genetic variants at the single-molecule level, revealing how sequence changes reshape distal regulatory coordination. Together, this sequence-to-distribution framework lays the foundation for understanding how genomic sequence encodes stochastic and dynamic genome regulation, and how genetic variation changes it, one molecule at a time.

papers.title: Roost: Avian Influenza Host Genomics Resource
papers.abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) causes mass mortality in poultry and wildlife, and puts already threatened species at further risk. Understanding differences in host susceptibility requires evidence currently scattered across publications, surveillance reports and genomic resources. We present Roost, a web resource that brings together more than 1,300 publications and reports, surveillance detections, and a catalogue of over 2,000 avian genome assemblies. Large language model-assisted literature analysis and comparative genomics link species, genes and molecular mechanisms to their supporting evidence. Around 51% of species with HPAI detections are not represented in the analysed corpus. Research concentrates on poultry, model organisms, and a small set of immune pathways. Research tracks neither mortality magnitude nor extinction risk; species with the largest recorded die-offs and threatened hosts alike remain largely unstudied. Roost makes this evidence, along with genome analyses, accessible to researchers and conservation practitioners, connecting documented disease with host biology and highlighting priorities for sequencing and functional research. Roost is available at http://josephguhlin.com/Roost

papers.title: Single-Cell RNA Sequencing Reveals Distinct Cellular and Molecular Features of Steroid-Induced Osteonecrosis of the Femoral Head Compared to Alcohol-Induced Osteonecrosis and Hip Osteoarthritis
papers.abstract: Osteonecrosis of the femoral head (ONFH) remains a devastating complication of glucocorticoid therapy and alcohol abuse, yet the pathophysiology is poorly understood. Using single-cell RNA sequencing, we analyzed femoral head specimens from patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty due to steroid-induced ONFH, alcohol-induced ONFH, or hip osteoarthritis (OA). Our comprehensive analysis across conditions revealed etiology-specific cellular compositions and transcriptional profiles. Steroid-induced ONFH demonstrated a distinctive immunological signature characterized by a neutrophil-predominant, elevated innate-to-adaptive immune cell ratio compared to alcohol-induced ONFH or OA. T cell analysis revealed impaired maturation in steroid-induced ONFH, with abundant naive T cells but reduced mature CD4+ T cells and CD4+ memory T cells compared to both alcohol-induced ONFH and OA. In addition, compared to alcohol-induced ONFH, steroid-induced ONFH was associated with an increase in exhausted/dysfunctional CD8+ T cells which suggests an impaired response to stress and reflects chronic immune dysfunction. Within stromal cell populations, steroid-induced ONFH demonstrated an increase in pericytes, endothelial cells, and mesenchymal cell with osteogenic features as compared to both alcohol-induced ONFH or OA. These findings collectively reveal novel cellular mechanisms underlying steroid-induced ONFH which may contribute to further investigation of etiology-specific pathogenesis and treatment strategies.

papers.title: Cross-species epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity: Insights from Jonathan the Giant Tortoise and human centenarians
papers.abstract: Can epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity transcend species boundaries? By comparing findings from a previously published epigenomic study of Jonathan, a 194-year-old giant tortoise, based on buccal scrape and saliva samples, with the analyses of publicly available DNA methylation data from exceptionally long-lived humans based on peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), this comparative study reveals intriguing molecular parallels across evolutionarily distant species. Human individuals aged 110+ years exhibited significantly higher global methylation entropy than those aged 60-82 years. Furthermore, 12 candidate genes displayed a distinctive promoter methylation entropy profile, with lower values at the youngest and oldest ages than in intermediate-age groups. Strikingly, these genes were enriched in telomere-related biological processes, highlighting a compelling link between epigenomic patterns and pathways implicated in aging. The correspondence between the findings in humans and previously reported observations in Jonathan suggests testable hypotheses about epigenomic signatures of exceptional longevity that may be conserved across species and extend beyond tissue-specific effects.

papers.title: Comparative molecular analysis of histopathologic subtypes reveals shared epithelial remodeling yet distinct fibroblast programs in scleroderma lung disease
papers.abstract: Rationale: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) drives mortality in systemic sclerosis (SSc), with a subset developing progressive pulmonary fibrosis (PPF) resembling idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis (IPF). Despite recognition of two distinct histopathologic patterns, the cellular basis of nonspecific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP) and usual interstitial pneumonia (UIP) remains poorly understood. Objectives: To define shared and distinct cellular and molecular features of SSc-NSIP and SSc-UIP compared to IPF. Methods: Single-nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics were performed on explanted lungs from patients with SSc-NSIP (n=6), SSc-UIP (n=6), or IPF (n=6), and control donors (n=12) with immunohistochemistry and western blot validation. Main Results: Across 120,254 nuclei from 35 cell types, there was striking similarity across fibrotic subgroups in epithelial, endothelial, and immune compartments, including alveolar type 1 cell loss, pathologic alveolar type 2 (AT2) gene expression, and expansion of COL15A1 endothelial cells and profibrotic macrophages. Diseased AT2s showed activation of the p53/DNA damage pathway. Aberrant basaloid (AB) cells were present in both SSc-ILD subtypes and transcriptionally similar to IPF ABs. They consistently neighbored profibrotic CTHRC1 fibroblasts, even in SSc-NSIP, despite lacking fibroblast foci. Fibroblast heterogeneity differentiated the histopathologic subtypes. Inflammatory fibroblasts were enriched in SSc-NSIP and CTHRC1 fibroblasts in UIP. AB-to-pathologic fibroblast crosstalk was defined by profibrotic signaling, with amplified TGF-{beta} signaling in UIP. Conclusions: Convergent epithelial remodeling is a hallmark of PPF in SSc-ILD and IPF. Fibroblast heterogeneity characterized by altered TGF-beta signaling distinguishes SSc-NSIP from SSc-UIP and IPF. Accelerated aging, DNA damage, and p53-dependent senescence pathways may represent shared drivers of PPF.

papers.title: GPBench: A benchmark framework for genomic prediction
papers.abstract: Genomic prediction (GP) has emerged as a powerful data mining strategy for disease risk assessment and molecular breeding. GP leverages genome-wide genetic variations and phenotypic information through a computational model to estimate genetic potential or disease risk. However, the field of GP still faces several major challenges: (i) dataset bias and insufficient representativeness; (ii) the lack of standardized evaluation protocols and a systematic benchmarking framework; (iii) heavy reliance on empirical expertise for experimental result interpretation, which hinders large-scale and systematic analysis. These issues make it difficult to conduct systematic cross-species evaluation and comparison of GP methods, and their authentic applications. To address these challenges, we established a standardized and extensible GP benchmark framework-GPBench. We first collected and harmonized public datasets from 16 species, covering animals, plants, and microorganisms, comprising 57 traits, 40,821 samples, and 493,821 single-nucleotide polymorphisms. Then, using the standardized datasets, the framework evaluates 21 GP models and provides a unified assessment across four dimensions: effectiveness, sensitivity, robustness, and scalability. Furthermore, we developed a large language model-based intelligent analysis system to facilitate the interpretation of GP experiments and model recommendations. GPBench provides the community with a fair, unified, and scalable platform (https://www.sdu-idea.cn/GPBench/) and an open-source library for comparing and optimizing GP methods, ultimately accelerating the application of GP in life sciences and biomedical research.

papers.title: Chromosome folding encodes mechanisms of cohesion maintenance
papers.abstract: After DNA replication, sister chromatids are physically linked by the cohesin complex. These cohesin linkages must be maintained for many hours for faithful chromosome segregation and DNA repair. Cohesin interacts with multiple rapidly exchanging cofactors, including SORORIN, which is often described as a molecular lock for cohesin on chromatin. How such transient SORORIN binding can protect cohesin over much longer timescales remains mechanistically unclear. Furthermore, how loop-extruding cohesins interact with and influence the positioning of sister-linking cohesins remains largely unknown. Here we show that changes in sister chromatid folding over time and after perturbations encode distinct signatures of the underlying mechanisms of cohesion maintenance. By integrating biochemical kinetics with polymer modeling, we infer cohesin turnover, motion, and encounter rules from these folding signatures. Repeated transient sequestration by SORORIN enables long-lasting protection yet acts as a quantitative modulator, rather than a binary switch for cohesion maintenance. Prolonging cohesin residence time by WAPL depletion exposes additional mechanisms shaping sister chromatid conformation, including pushing of sister-linking cohesins and diffusion of loop-extruding cohesins. Together, these results reveal how transient cofactor interactions regulate long-lived cohesin maintenance and establish sister chromosome organization as a quantitative readout of otherwise hidden molecular mechanisms.

papers.title: Synthetic MPRA perturbation supervision improves variant-effect prediction in sequence-to-function models
papers.abstract: Deep learning sequence-to-function (S2F) models learn to predict functional readouts, such as gene expression, from genetic sequence. However, these models are trained predominantly on the reference genome and struggle to accurately predict the effect of genetic variation on gene expression. Massively parallel reporter assays (MPRAs) explore the direct impact of genetic variation on gene expression, but saturation-mutagenesis MPRAs that measure variant effects directly remain limited, thereby restricting their use for fine-tuning S2F models. In this work, we investigate fine-tuning Borzoi, a state-of-the-art S2F model, on model-generated synthetic MPRA variant-effect data as a scalable alternative to overcome limits on the availability of supervised training data for genetic variation. First, we trained an ensemble of 16 models on 110,359 K562 MPRA measurements. Then, we distilled their predictions into a single student model using MPRA elements associated with 1,000 genes. The distilled model was subsequently used to generate synthetic variant-effect labels across increasing numbers of genes (50 to 1,000), with 600 variants per gene, to fine-tune Borzoi. Performance improved as we included more genes in training. In data-limited settings, training on more genes with fewer variants per gene performed better than training on fewer genes with more variants per gene, given the same number of total variants. Compared to pre-trained Borzoi, Borzoi fine-tuned on 600,000 synthetic samples across 1,000 genes increased Pearson correlation from 0.28 to 0.54 on CAGI5 promoter variants and from 0.39 to 0.46 on 903 GTEx fine-mapped whole-blood expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs). Importantly, these improvements were achieved while preserving the pre-trained performance across all 7,611 output tracks. Furthermore, fine-tuned Borzoi recovered regulatory motifs identified by the MPRA model in genes unseen during training, suggesting that learned regulatory features can generalize across loci. Together, these results provide a proof of concept that model-generated synthetic supervision can improve variant effect prediction in S2F models while preserving their original pre-trained capabilities, offering a scalable strategy toward capturing the impact of genetic variation on gene regulation.

papers.title: A generative network model reveals hierarchical structural memory guiding post-mitotic 3D genome inheritance
papers.abstract: How three-dimensional (3D) genome organization is reestablished after mitosis to preserve gene regulatory programs and cell identity remains unresolved. We asked whether mitotic chromosome architecture contributes to cellular memory by preserving structural information while maintaining the flexibility required for cellular adaptation. Here we introduce HiCONA, a generative Bayesian framework that infers hierarchical genome organization and quantifies the structural contribution of individual interactions through an Entropy Impact Score. HiCONA resolves genome organization across multiple scales, revealing structure-defining interaction patterns underlying chromatin architecture, independently of experimental modality. We identify structurally impactful chromatin interactions retained during mitosis delineating distinct trajectories of post-mitotic genome reassembly. These mitotically preserved interactions are enriched for active, transcriptionally competent regulatory elements, consistent with a cis-encoded architectural memory subsequently remodeled by trans-acting regulators. Together, our findings suggest that molecular information retained on mitotic chromosomes guides structural trajectories, providing an architectural basis for epigenetic memory and post-mitotic genome inheritance.

papers.title: Ancient U/V sex chromosomes reveal slow expansion of recombination suppression in Polytrichaceae mosses.
papers.abstract: Sex chromosomes evolving in haploid versus diploid life cycles provide complementary systems for testing theories of sex chromosome evolution, yet haploid sex chromosomes remain poorly studied. In dioicous bryophytes, females and males carry non-recombining U and V chromosomes, respectively, providing a unique opportunity to examine the consequences of long-term recombination suppression independently of diploid heterogamety. Here, we characterize the U/V sex chromosomes of Polytrichaceae using chromosome-scale genomes from ten species. We identify homologous U/V chromosomes across the family and show that their non-recombining sex-determining regions (SDRs) originated early in Polytrichaceae evolution, approximately 124 million years ago. Despitetheir ancient origin, however, the SDRs have undergone limited expansion and are consistently flanked by large pseudoautosomal regions (PARs). The SDRs nevertheless show strong genomic signatures of recombination suppression, including reduced gene density, transposable-element accumulation, reduced diversity, high synonymous divergence, and altered codon usage. Yet they retain hundreds of genes and show limited evidence of functional degeneration. Their gene content is dynamic, with frequent lineage-specific gains and losses, while a conserved core of 60 orthogroups has persisted across all ten species for more than 100 million years. Comparisons across sex chromosome systems suggest that haploid U/V chromosomes retain more genes than similarly old diploid X/Y or Z/W chromosomes, consistent with a role for haploid selection in limiting degeneration. However, haploid selection alone cannot explain the limited SDR expansion observed in Polytrichaceae, suggesting that other factors also shape SDR evolution. Together, these results reveal an ancient U/V system in which recombination suppression has strong genomic consequences but has not driven extensive SDR expansion or functional degeneration. By decoupling recombination suppression from diploid heterogamety, U/V chromosomes provide a powerful framework for distinguishing the consequences of recombination arrest from those of ploidy in sex chromosome evolution.

papers.title: Local chromatin, 3D genome folding and transposon cargo shape Sleeping Beauty transposition
papers.abstract: The cut-and-paste DNA transposon Sleeping Beauty (SB) is widely used for genome engineering, mutagenesis and gene delivery. When mobilized from a genomic donor position ("launch site"), SB preferentially reintegrates locally (< 2 Mb), but factors governing its transposition from genomic sites remain incompletely understood. Here we analysed local transposition experiments in mouse embryonic stem cells to determine the influence of chromatin context and transposon cargo on SB transposition. Transposons in launch sites with transcriptionally active, accessible chromatin showed lower transposition efficiency. Large cargo and cargo with higher transcriptional activity also result in reduced transposition efficiency. After excision, local reintegration patterns closely resembled 3D contact frequencies of the launch site. This indicates that chromosome folding is a major determinant of the transposition pattern. Surprisingly, we did not detect any effect of the destination chromatin composition on reintegration efficiency. Cargo sequence modified the reintegration patterns: promoter-containing cargo increased both very proximal (<10kb) and interchromosomal transpositions, while CTCF binding sites in the cargo increased reintegration on the launch chromosome. Together, these results define key determinants of SB transposition in chromosomes and inform the design of SB-based genome engineering strategies.

papers.title: Urban enrichment of molestus ancestry and opposing temperature clines in a metropolitan Culex pipiens hybrid zone
papers.abstract: Hybridization between ecologically distinct lineages can fuel rapid adaptation when introgressed alleles are locally favored. The North American Culex pipiens assemblage, a principal West Nile virus vector east of the Mississippi, comprises three lineages---temperate Cx. pipiens f. pipiens, urban-specialist Cx. pipiens f. molestus, and subtropical Cx. quinquefasciatus---that meet in a mid-Atlantic hybrid zone where temperature and urbanization gradients intersect. Using whole-genome Pool-seq of 24 field populations and three lineage-reference pools across the Baltimore--Washington corridor, we find a weakly differentiated, Cx. pipiens f. pipiens-like background, richer in molestus- and quinquefasciatus-like ancestry toward the warmer end of the corridor. Urbanization impacts allele frequencies across the genome: molestus-like ancestry rises with impervious surface, independently of temperature and position, while Cx. quinquefasciatus-like ancestry does not. An 11.6 Mb chromosome 3 inversion is molestus-like in every population, most of all in urban ones, and tracks genome-wide molestus-like ancestry. Temperature acts locus by locus. On chromosome 1, a cluster of six CYP6 paralogs, a family implicated in insecticide resistance and thermal-stress response, shows rising Cx. quinquefasciatus-like ancestry and read depth with temperature. A chromosome 2 interval centered on a Yan ortholog, a repressor of cell differentiation, shows non-quinquefasciatus ancestry increasing with temperature, consistent with selection against Cx. quinquefasciatus-like introgression. Urban populations therefore carry more ancestry from the human-commensal lineage, while temperature moves ancestry both ways at individual loci. Both molestus and Cx. quinquefasciatus donors carry human-contact traits, so these patterns bear on how warming and urbanization will reshape arboviral risk.

papers.title: Transcriptional contingency in the early hematopoiesis of inherited bone marrow failure syndromes
papers.abstract: The inherited bone marrow failure syndromes (IBMFS) are a group of heterogeneous genetic diseases caused by germline pathogenic variants in genes involved in hematopoiesis and genomic integrity. Despite sharing common phenotypical manifestations that have aided opportune diagnosis, such as bone marrow failure, congenital malformations and an increased predisposition to develop cancer, little is known about the shared and distinctive transcriptional programs in their hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells compartment that underlie the clinical manifestations of each disease. In this work we have successfully integrated and analyzed the publicly available scRNAseq datasets of HSPCs from patients with Fanconi anemia (FA) and Telomere Biology disorders (TBD), as well as healthy controls. Once integrated, we performed quality control metrics, as well as batch effect correction using different methods. Through dimensionality reduction, cell clustering and cell type annotation we found distinctive gene expression profiles per syndrome and per cell type, as well as orchestrated gene expression profiles, including upregulation of inflammatory pathways and cell proliferation pathways. This work shows the integration of datasets from FA and TBD, two major IBMFS, and provides the basis for an accumulative, comparative, and integrated atlas of scRNAseq data from patients with IBMFS.
